# Endorois case

The **Endorois case** is a landmark human rights decision by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) concerning the rights of the Endorois, an indigenous pastoralist community in Kenya. The case, formally titled *Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya*, was submitted to the ACHPR in 2003 and decided on 25 November 2009, with adoption by the African Union on 2 February 2010. The case has been recognized as a foundational decision in African and international human rights law for establishing the first African legal recognition of indigenous peoples' collective rights to ancestral lands and for issuing the first international ruling on the right to development.

# Background

### The Endorois Community

The Endorois are a semi-nomadic pastoralist community of approximately 60,000 people who lived for centuries in the Lake Bogoria region of the Central Rift Valley in Kenya. Their way of life was inextricably linked to the land around Lake Bogoria, where they grazed cattle, sheep, and goats, and practiced beekeeping. The community relied on the fertile lands surrounding the lake, which provided green pastures and medicinal salt licks essential for raising healthy livestock. Lake Bogoria held profound religious and cultural significance for the Endorois, serving as the location of sacred prayer sites, circumcision ritual sites, and other ceremonial grounds used regularly throughout the year. The Endorois believed that the spirits of deceased community members resided in the lake and held annual festivals there with participation from Endorois across the region. The Monchongoi Forest was considered the birthplace of the Endorois people and the settlement of the first Endorois community.

Under British colonial administration and continuing after Kenyan independence in 1963, the land around Lake Bogoria was held in trust for the Endorois community. The Endorois maintained customary ownership and use of the land without significant challenge until the 1970s.

### Displacement and Initial Remedies

In November 1973, the Kenyan government gazzetted the Lake Bogoria area as a game reserve (initially called the Lake Hannington Game Reserve, later renamed the Lake Bogoria Game Reserve and re-gazetted in 1978) without consulting the Endorois community. The creation of the game reserve was intended to promote wildlife conservation and tourism development. Approximately 400 Endorois families were forcibly removed from their land beginning in 1973, with additional evictions occurring in 1983.

When Kenyan Wildlife Service (KWS) officials informed Endorois elders of the eviction, they allegedly promised that 400 Endorois families would receive plots of fertile land as compensation, that the community would receive 25 percent of tourism revenue from the game reserve, that 85 percent of employment opportunities would go to the Endorois, and that the government would construct cattle dips and fresh water dams for the community. These promises were largely unfulfilled. By 1986, only 170 of the 400 families received minimal financial compensation, which officials characterized as relocation assistance rather than compensation for the loss of ancestral lands. The Endorois were relocated to semi-arid areas where the majority of their livestock did not survive, and where access to potable water remained limited.

In 1986, the Endorois community petitioned President Daniel arap Moi for redress. Following a meeting with Endorois leaders in December 1994 at his Lake Bogoria Hotel, President Moi ordered that the government respect the 1973 compensation agreement and directed that 25 percent of annual income from the game reserve be allocated to community projects. However, these directives were not implemented. When the Endorois requested a follow-up meeting in 1995, President Moi again ordered implementation of his directives, but government compliance remained minimal.

In response to the government's failure to implement presidential directives, the Endorois filed a case with the High Court of Kenya in 2000. The High Court decided the case on 19 April 2002, ruling in favor of the government. The court found that the procedures for establishing the game reserve had been followed properly and that the minimal compensation paid in 1986 fulfilled any government obligation to the Endorois. The High Court explicitly stated that it could not address the question of a community's collective right to property, focusing instead on individual claimants. The court concluded that Kenyan law did not provide special protection for land claims based on historical occupation and cultural rights.

### Additional Grievances

After the High Court decision, conditions for the Endorois deteriorated further. In 2002, the Kenyan government began granting concessions to private ruby mining companies to extract minerals from Endorois ancestral lands. This mining activity created significant risks of contaminating water sources used by the Endorois for drinking and livestock watering. Additionally, the government demarcated and sold portions of Endorois land to third parties without consultation with the community.

# Proceeding Before the African Commission

### Filing and Admissibility

On 22 May 2003, the Centre for Minority Rights Development (CEMIRIDE), a Kenyan civil rights organization, filed a formal letter of intent with the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, submitting a communication on behalf of the Endorois Welfare Council (EWC). The communication was supported by Minority Rights Group International (MRG), a London-based international organization focused on minority and indigenous rights, and received an amicus curiae brief from the Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (CORE). The complainants alleged that Kenya had violated Articles 8, 14, 17, 21, and 22 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights through its forced removal of the Endorois, failure to provide adequate compensation, and denial of participation in decisions affecting their land.

The Kenyan government initially failed to submit written responses on admissibility despite repeated reminders from the African Commission. At its 37th Ordinary Session in May 2005, the ACHPR declared the communication admissible, finding that the Endorois community had exhausted available domestic remedies and that the case met the admissibility criteria under Article 56 of the African Charter. The decision on admissibility was issued despite Kenya's failure to cooperate with the procedural requirements.

### Consideration of Merits

Following the admissibility decision, both parties submitted arguments on the merits of the case. The African Commission heard oral testimony from expert witnesses and representatives of both parties at its 40th Ordinary Session in November 2006. The case involved complex questions about the nature of indigenous peoples' rights, the definition of the "right to development," and the extent to which international human rights law protected collective land rights. Consideration of the merits was deferred through subsequent sessions before the African Commission rendered its final decision in November 2009 at its 46th Ordinary Session.

# Decision

### Recognition of Endorois as a "People"

A foundational aspect of the ACHPR's decision was its recognition of the Endorois as a distinct indigenous "people" entitled to bring collective claims for rights under the African Charter. Kenya argued that the Endorois were merely a sub-tribe of the larger Tugen or Kalenjin groups and therefore not entitled to protection as a distinct people under the Charter. The ACHPR rejected this argument, finding that the Endorois had satisfied the criteria for recognition as an indigenous people: they had a continuous historical presence in the Lake Bogoria region, maintained a distinct cultural identity and pastoralist way of life dependent on the land, had a traditional system of governance through elders and the EWC, and had been marginalized in relation to state power. The commission relied on precedent from the Ogoni case (*The Social and Economic Rights Action Centre for Economic and Social Rights v. Nigeria*), which established that indigenous peoples and other communities could bring collective claims before the ACHPR.

### Violations Found

The ACHPR found that Kenya violated five articles of the African Charter:

**Article 8 (Right to Practice Religion)**: The commission ruled that Kenya violated the Endorois' right to freedom of conscience and religion by denying the community access to Lake Bogoria and surrounding sacred sites essential to their religious practices. The commission rejected Kenya's argument that restricting access was necessary for conservation purposes, finding no significant public interest justification that would warrant such a comprehensive denial of religious practice. The commission noted that the religious sites had not been properly demarcated or protected within the game reserve.

**Article 14 (Right to Property)**: The ACHPR recognized that the Endorois' ancestral land held under the Kenyan Constitution's trust land system constituted "property" within the meaning of the African Charter, even though ownership was not documented through written title. The commission found that Kenya violated this right by encroaching on Endorois property without a legal basis proportionate to any legitimate government objective. The commission held that the government had failed to adequately negotiate with the Endorois before limiting their access and had provided compensation that was "wholly inadequate" and "[flew] in the face of common sense and fairness." The commission also found that Kenya's eviction of the Endorois violated the requirement of legality and proportionality, as conservation of the game reserve could have been achieved through the involvement of the Endorois rather than their removal.

**Article 17 (Right to Culture)**: The commission found that Kenya violated the Endorois' right to develop, protect, and promote their culture by removing them from the land and severely restricting their access to sites essential to their cultural identity and traditional pastoralist way of life. The commission noted that the African Charter requires states to provide for "the conservation, development and diffusion of culture" without exceptions that would allow eviction of indigenous communities.

**Article 21 (Right to Free Disposition of Natural Resources)**: The ACHPR found that Kenya violated the Endorois' right to use and benefit from their natural resources by restricting their access to salt licks, pastures, and other resources on their ancestral land. The commission ruled that the restriction was not in the public interest, as a meaningful way to achieve conservation would have been to involve the Endorois, who, as inhabitants of the land, would be "best equipped to maintain its delicate ecosystems." The commission found that Kenya had also failed to provide the Endorois with any benefit from economic activities on their land, including tourism revenue and ruby mining concessions.

**Article 22 (Right to Development)**: The ACHPR's analysis of the right to development was landmark, as it represented the first international human rights tribunal decision finding a violation of this right. The commission formulated a definition of the right to development as both "constitutive and instrumental," meaning it must satisfy tests of both procedural and substantive law. The commission held that development activities on Endorois land violated this right because: the Endorois were not consulted or granted free, prior, and informed consent; they had no meaningful participation in decisions affecting the land; and the development resulted in harm rather than empowerment of the community, causing loss of access to resources necessary for their economic and social development. The commission rejected Kenya's argument that indirect participation through the democratic system was sufficient, finding that meaningful participation required direct dialogue with and explicit consent from the affected community.

### Remedies

The ACHPR recommended that the Kenyan government take the following actions:

1. Recognize the Endorois' ownership of their ancestral lands and ensure their restitution with legal title and clear demarcation.
2. Ensure the Endorois have unrestricted access to Lake Bogoria for religious ceremonies, cultural practices, and grazing of livestock.
3. Provide adequate compensation to the community for all losses suffered through the loss of property, disruption of pastoral enterprise, and denial of religious and cultural rights.
4. Pay royalties to the Endorois from economic activities on the land, including tourism revenue and any mining operations.
5. Register the Endorois Welfare Council as a representative organization.
6. Engage in dialogue with the Endorois community to discuss implementation of these remedies and submit a report on implementation within three months.

The ACHPR offered its good offices to facilitate implementation of its decision.

# Significance and Impact

### Precedent for Indigenous Rights

The Endorois case is widely regarded as a watershed moment for indigenous rights in Africa. It was the first decision by an African human rights body to legally recognize indigenous peoples' collective rights over traditionally owned land. The decision affirmed that indigenous communities could hold land rights even in the absence of written documentation and that customary tenure systems were entitled to protection under international human rights law. The case established that states must obtain free, prior, and informed consent from indigenous peoples before undertaking development projects or extracting resources from their lands.

### Right to Development

The ACHPR's articulation of the right to development was landmark in global human rights law. Before the Endorois decision, the right to development had been recognized in international instruments such as the UN Declaration on the Right to Development, but had not been the subject of a binding judicial decision by an international tribunal. The Endorois case established important principles: that development must be participatory and benefit the affected community; that development cannot be imposed without the consent of indigenous peoples; and that the right to development includes both procedural components (consultation and participation) and substantive components (ensuring that development actually empowers communities rather than harming them).

The decision has influenced subsequent cases on indigenous land rights in Kenya and across Africa, including the Ogiek case against Kenya. Both the Endorois and Ogiek decisions established precedent that conservation and development objectives do not justify the denial of indigenous peoples' rights to their ancestral lands and resources.

### Constitutional Impact

The ACHPR's decision contributed to the debate surrounding Kenya's constitutional reform process. In 2010, Kenya adopted a new constitution that recognized collective land rights and indigenous peoples' rights. The National Guidelines for Free, Prior, and Informed Consent, issued by Kenya's Ministry of Environment in 2016, explicitly reflected the ACHPR's jurisprudence from the Endorois case.

### International Advocacy

The case generated significant international attention and advocacy concerning indigenous land rights. The decision was adopted by the African Union and endorsed by various United Nations human rights bodies. In 2016, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights expressed concern in its Concluding Observations on Kenya that the government had not implemented the Endorois decision and recommended immediate implementation. In 2017, the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination similarly called upon Kenya to ensure legal recognition of the Endorois' collective rights and to implement the African Commission's decision.

# Implementation

### Limited Compliance

Despite the ACHPR's clear recommendations and the African Union's adoption of the decision, Kenya's implementation has been limited. As of 2024, the Kenyan government had not fully complied with the decision's core requirements.

Access and Management: The Endorois have been granted limited access to Lake Bogoria without entrance fees, but access remains discretionary and is managed by the game reserve authorities rather than being an assured right. In 2011, Lake Bogoria was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site without consultation with the Endorois, which prompted advocacy and a State of Conservation report from the World Heritage Committee in 2014 requiring the inclusion of the Endorois in management and benefit-sharing arrangements. Following advocacy efforts, the Endorois signed a memorandum of understanding with the Kenya Wildlife Service and Baringo County Council recognizing Lake Bogoria as Endorois ancestral land and requiring Endorois inclusion in land management decisions. However, implementation of this memorandum in practice has been incomplete.

Compensation: The government has provided limited financial compensation and revenue sharing, but not at the levels recommended by the ACHPR. The Endorois were promised 25 percent of tourism revenue, but revenue-sharing arrangements remain far below this level and are subject to government discretion.

Land Restitution: The Endorois have not been granted full ownership of their ancestral lands or complete restitution, despite the clear recommendation in the ACHPR decision. Some land has been allocated to the Endorois for specific purposes, such as a cultural center at the entrance to the reserve, but full recognition of ancestral land rights has not occurred.

### Advocacy and International Pressure

Since the 2009 decision, civil society organizations and indigenous rights advocates have pursued ongoing advocacy to pressure the Kenyan government to implement the ACHPR's recommendations. The African Commission issued a resolution in 2013 calling on Kenya to implement the Endorois decision and faced criticism for lack of government compliance. In 2014, Kenya established a government task force to study implementation of the Endorois decision with an initial one-year mandate, though this task force did not lead to comprehensive implementation. Organizations including Minority Rights Group International, the Centre for Minority Rights Development, the Kenya Human Rights Commission, and the Endorois Welfare Council have coordinated advocacy efforts, conducted community workshops, and worked with the ACHPR and United Nations bodies to press for implementation.

The Endorois community has continued to face challenges with implementation efforts. As of 2025, fourteen years after the ACHPR decision, many of the commission's core recommendations remained unfulfilled, including full land restitution, adequate compensation, and assured revenue sharing.

### Related Cases

The precedent established in the Endorois case influenced subsequent indigenous land rights litigation in Africa. The Ogiek case, brought against Kenya for the eviction of the Ogiek people from the Mau Forest, was directly informed by the Endorois decision. In 2017, the African Court of Human and Peoples' Rights issued a decision on the Ogiek case recognizing the Ogiek's rights to their ancestral lands, and in 2022, the African Court ordered Kenya to pay reparations to the Ogiek. Both the Endorois and Ogiek decisions have become reference points for indigenous peoples' land rights litigation across the African continent.

In 2010, Kenya adopted a new constitution that recognized indigenous peoples' rights.
The National Guidelines for Free, Prior, and Informed Consent, issued by Kenya's Ministry of Environment in 2016, explicitly reflected the ACHPR's jurisprudence from the Endorois case.
The Endorois case generated significant international attention concerning indigenous land rights.
The Endorois case generated significant international advocacy concerning indigenous land rights.
The decision was adopted by the African Union.
The decision was endorsed by various United Nations human rights bodies.
In 2016, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights expressed concern in its Concluding Observations on Kenya that the government had not implemented the Endorois decision.
The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recommended immediate implementation of the Endorois decision.
In 2017, the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination similarly called upon Kenya to ensure legal recognition of the Endorois' collective rights.
In 2017, the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination similarly called upon Kenya to implement the African Commission's decision.
Despite the ACHPR's clear recommendations, Kenya's implementation has been limited.
Despite the African Union's adoption of the decision, Kenya's implementation has been limited.
As of 2024, the Kenyan government had not fully complied with the decision's core requirements.
The Endorois have been granted limited access to Lake Bogoria without entrance fees.
Access to Lake Bogoria remains discretionary.
Access to Lake Bogoria is managed by the game reserve authorities rather than being an assured right.
In 2011, Lake Bogoria was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site without consultation with the Endorois.
The designation of Lake Bogoria as a UNESCO World Heritage Site prompted advocacy.
The designation of Lake Bogoria as a UNESCO World Heritage Site prompted a State of Conservation report from the World Heritage Committee in 2014.
The State of Conservation report required the inclusion of the Endorois in management arrangements.
The State of Conservation report required the inclusion of the Endorois in benefit-sharing arrangements.
Following advocacy efforts, the Endorois signed a memorandum of understanding with the Kenya Wildlife Service.
Following advocacy efforts, the Endorois signed a memorandum of understanding with Baringo County Council.
The memorandum of understanding recognized Lake Bogoria as Endorois ancestral land.
The memorandum of understanding required Endorois inclusion in land management decisions.
Implementation of this memorandum in practice has been incomplete.
The government has provided limited financial compensation.
The government has provided limited revenue sharing.
Financial compensation and revenue sharing are not at the levels recommended by the ACHPR.
The Endorois were promised 25 percent of tourism revenue.
Revenue-sharing arrangements remain far below the promised 25 percent level.
Revenue-sharing arrangements are subject to government discretion.
The Endorois have not been granted full ownership of their ancestral lands.
The Endorois have not been granted complete restitution of their ancestral lands, despite the clear recommendation in the ACHPR decision.
Some land has been allocated to the Endorois for specific purposes, such as a cultural center at the entrance to the reserve.
Full recognition of ancestral land rights has not occurred for the Endorois.
Since the 2009 decision, civil society organizations have pursued ongoing advocacy to pressure the Kenyan government to implement the ACHPR's recommendations.
Indigenous rights advocates have pursued ongoing advocacy to pressure the Kenyan government to implement the ACHPR's recommendations.
The African Commission issued a resolution in 2013 calling on Kenya to implement the Endorois decision.
The African Commission faced criticism for lack of government compliance.
In 2014, Kenya established a government task force to study implementation of the Endorois decision with an initial one-year mandate.
This task force did not lead to comprehensive implementation.
Organizations including Minority Rights Group International have coordinated advocacy efforts.
Organizations including the Centre for Minority Rights Development have coordinated advocacy efforts.
Organizations including the Kenya Human Rights Commission have coordinated advocacy efforts.
Organizations including the Endorois Welfare Council have coordinated advocacy efforts.
These organizations conducted community workshops.
These organizations worked with the ACHPR to press for implementation.
These organizations worked with United Nations bodies to press for implementation.
The Endorois community has continued to face challenges with implementation efforts.
As of 2025, fourteen years after the ACHPR decision, many of the commission's core recommendations remained unfulfilled.
Unfulfilled recommendations include full land restitution.
Unfulfilled recommendations include adequate compensation.
Unfulfilled recommendations include assured revenue sharing.
The precedent established in the Endorois case influenced subsequent indigenous land rights litigation in Africa.
The Ogiek case, brought against Kenya for the eviction of the Ogiek people from the Mau Forest, was directly informed by the Endorois decision.
In 2017, the African Court of Human and Peoples' Rights issued a decision on the Ogiek case recognizing the Ogiek's rights to their ancestral lands.
In 2022, the African Court ordered Kenya to pay reparations to the Ogiek.
Both the Endorois and Ogiek decisions have become reference points for indigenous peoples' land rights litigation across the African continent.

Latest

25 August 2010

The Endorois indigenous community in Kenya has successfully contested their eviction from their ancestral land by the Kenyan government. In a landmark decision adopted by the African Union on 2 February 2010, the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (‘the African Commission’) declared the expulsion of Endorois from their ancestral lands illegal. The African Commission found that the Kenyan government had violated certain fundamental rights of the Endorois community protected under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the ‘African Charter’) and other international instruments.

MRG’s briefing paper disects the ruling and looks at the wider implications for indigenous people in Kenya and beyond.

t



L

### The Jurisprudence behind the Right to Self-determination and Right to Development in the African Charter for Human and Peoples Rights.


lssa G. Shivji

Professor Emeritus

School of Law

University of Dar es Salaam


By way of lntroduction

# o ln this short presentation I want to focus on Peoples Rights in the African Charter.



o



The concept of Peoples Rights is the most innovative part of the African Charter


unlike many other regional human rights instruments; yet it has not received


sufficient attention from academics and regional human rights bodies, particularly in


recent decades. The Charter takes an integral view of the three generation of rights:


civil and political rights, social, economic and cultural rights and collective rights.



a I want to focus on the [jurisprudence ] of two peoples rights: right of peoples to self

determination (Art. 21) and the right to development (preamble and Art. zz(t)(z).



a



ln discussing the [jurisprudence ] of these two rights, I want to draw on the rich


jurisprudence developed by the African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights


(the Commission).


## o While the African Commission has discussed these rights in several cases,** I will

focus on one particular case where it discussed at great length the meaning and


purport of these two rights. This is the case of:


. Presentation to the lntergenerational Dialogue on the occasion of the 2023 Jud icial Year of the African Court
on Human and Peoples' Rights.
-. Among these are: The Social and Economic Rights Action Centre v Nigeria, Comm. L55lg6, (2OOO-2OO1|, The
ogoni Case, Katangese People's Congress v. Zaire, Comm. 75/92, (1994-1995), The Kotangese Cose, Democratic
Republic of Congo v Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, 277/99, The DRC cqse. All these decisions are available
online on the African Commission website.


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-1-full.png)

2



a



CENTRE FOR MINORTTY RTGHTS DEVETOPMENT [(KENYA) ] [AND ] [MINORIW ] [RIGHTS]


GROUP TNTERNATTONAL ON BEHALF OF ENDOROIS WETFARE COUNCIL [(ENDOROIS]


cAsE)***


l'll start with the meaning of [peoples ] in the African Charter.



Meaning of Peoples



a



At the outset let me make three observations:
## i) Nowhere the Charter defines the term 'peoples'. Although reading the


Charter as a whole it is not difficutt to draw a working definition of the term.


ii) The term 'people' is in plural; not in singular thus implying that it refers to


peoples within the state with their own specific identity.


iii) The Charter does not use the term 'indigenous' which is the term commonly


used in the West-Centric human rights discourse derived from the reality of


the Americas where the original inhabitants of the continents were more or


less decimated by European invaders. The remnants are now called


'indigenous people', not citizens.


Of course, many of us know or should know, that the term 'indigenous' in


West dominated historiography has several connotations including


'backward, uncivilised people' which flies in the face of real history of these


people. But I will not go into it here except caution you that in Africa when we


use this term, we should be both circumspect and cautious.



.-. Briefly the facts were: Endorois pastoralist people were forcibly removed from their ancestral lands around

Lake Bogoria by the Government of Kenya to make way for Game Reserve [gazetted ] by the Government. The
land around Lake Bogoria provided Endorois with medicinalsalt licks which helped to raise healthy cattle. The

Lake Bogoria was also the site of ancestralworship, religious festivities and traditional rituals. Endrois [people]

believe that the spirits of Endorois [people ] live in Lake Bogoria. The Complainants thus alleged breach of several
Articlesof theAfricanCharterincluding Art.t4 (righttoproperty), Ati.22(righttoculture), Art.2L(rightto
natural resources) and several other Articles.


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-2-full.png)

3


To be sure, in the Endorois case, the Commission does use the word


'indigenous' since it is enjoined to draw inspiration from international human


rights instruments (Art. 60 ) but it uses it alternatively with 'peoples'. While


recognising that the terms 'peoples' and 'indigenous' are contentious, the


Commission was of the opinion that there are certain criteria which help to


identify'peoples'. And these are:


(i) 'the occupation and use of certain territory'. ln this the Commission


recognised link with ancestral land as an important ingredient in


identifying 'peoples'- where land is not only the site of livelihood but


also of religious and cultural practices.

## (ii) 'the voluntary perpetuation of cultural distinctiveness';


(iii) 'self-identification as a distinct collectivity, as well as recognition by


other groups';

## (iv) ' an experience of subjugation, marginalisation, dispossession,


exclusion and discrimination'. This is well captured in the term


'oppressed peoples'used in Art. 20 of the Charter.


Now I turn to the right of self-determination.


Right of Self- Determ ination



a



The right of self-determination is unambiguously recognised by the Charter. Art. 20

##### provides - and this is worth quoting in full.


Art. 21: 'All peoples shall have right to existence. They shall have the


unquestionable and inalienable right to self-determination. They shall freely


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-3-full.png)

a



4


determine their [political ] status and shall [pursue ] their economic and social


development according to the [poliry ] they have freely chosen."


I would like to make three observations on this:
## i) The right to self-determination is linked to right to life, in this case right to life


as a collective. And right to life, as you know, is one right which cannot e


derogated from.


ii) The right to self-determination cannot be subjected to restrictions or


exceptions or derogated from.


iii) The right to self-determination includes the right to make your own policies,


choose your political status and your path of development.


The importance of this cannot be overstated particularly in the current


international situation where African states are subjected to the dictates of


imperialist states and the so-called "development partners".


There are two aspects of the right to self-determination: external and internal.


External refers to the right of peoples to independence and sovereignty of colonised


people. I suggest that this right should not be read as a one-off right, that is, once


you have attained independence the right is exhausted. This is a continuous right and


continues to subsist in the peoples. Why do I say so?


Art. 2X(X) is read together with the preamble which stipulates total liberation of


Africa' and gives an 'undertaking to eliminate colonialism, neo-colonialism,


apartheid, zionism [yes, zionism], and to dismantle aggressive foreign military


bases...'. Again Art. 21(5) stipulates that State parties 'undertake to eliminate all


forms of economic exploitation particularly that practiced by international


monopolies so as to enable their peoples to fully benefit from the advantages


derived from their national resources'.


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-4-full.png)

a



5


As we knoq or should know, neo-colonialism and economic exploitation continue to


exist. Africa is not fully liberated and therefore the right to self-determination has not


been fully realized.


lnternal self-determination of the peoples refers to peoples within the State. They


also have the right to self-determination. Both, external and internal self

determination, are well captured in Art. 20 [(2l.where ] it is stipulated that'Colonized


or oppressed peoples shall have the right to free themselves from the bonds of


domination...', I suggest that the reference to oppressed [peoples ] is a reference to the

##### peoples inside a state - which is internal self-determination.



Next I turn to the right to development.


Right to Development



o


o



Art, 21(1) provides for a wholesome right to economic, social and cultural


development. All [peoples ] shall have the rightto their economic, social and cultural


development with due regard to their freedom and identity and in the equal


enjoyment of the common heritage of mankind.'


The African Commission in their decision in the Endorois case develops a profound


jurisprudence on this right.


Firstly, the Commission observed that the right to development is a 'two pronged


test, that is both constitutive and instrumental' or'useful as both the means and


end.' [(para ] .277). Thus the Commission held that it is not sufficient simply to look at


the end product, that ls development, but one must look at development os a


process in which the people concerned have participated fully and meaningfully.


### o Secondly by deepening the meaning and implication of participation, the

Commission linked the process of development to the right of self-determination.


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-5-full.png)

a


o


a



6


That is to say that the process of development is a particular manifestation of the


right of self-determination.


Thirdly, the Commission argued that the recognition of the right to development


'requires fulfilling five criteria: it must be equitable, non-discriminatory, participatory,


accou ntable, and transparent'. lpara. 277l.


These five criteria read together, I suggest, amount to defining the process of


development as a [participatory ] democratic development from below rather than


development imposed from above. And the process of development which fully


takes account of the right of self-determination of the people.


Fourthly, where the development involves taking land of the people concerned, as in


the case of Endorois, 'the State not only has a duty to consult with the community,


but also to obtain their free, prior and informed consent, according to their customs


and traditions'. [(para. ] 291)


Finolly, according to the Commission, development should result in the


empowerment of the people concerned and should expand the realm of their


capabilities and choices.


ln sum, the Commission is characterising development as a terrain of expanding the


realm of freedom of the people or what Mwalimu Nyerere once called 'Development


in Freedom'. Thus development and freedom are interdependent and mutually re

enforcing.



Conclusion


ln conclusion I would like to make two observations:

##### L. To the best of my knowledge, neither the African Court of Human and Peoples


Rights, nor the East African Court of Justice have drawn on the rich jurisprudence


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/1768107023614086732/1768107023614086732.pdf-6-full.png)

7



developed by the African Commission on collective rights, in particular the right of


peoples to self-determination and right to developmen! and customary property


rights to ancestral lands and destruction of cultural and religious sites as, for


example, often alleged by Maasai people in a number of cases filed before the EACJ

### 2. Secondly, the decisions of the African Commission have surprisingly not entered the


public legal and political discourse because legal and other academics, particularly in


Tanzania, with the exception of a few intellectual-activists, seem to pay little heed to


the plight of marginalised groups such as the Maasai of Loliondo.

### 3. lf this presentation of mine can generate some discussion on the series of decisions


collective rights of the African Commission it would have served its purpose.

##### *****

The Endorois and Ogiek communities are still waiting to return to their rightful ancestral lands. **Anthony Langat** reports.

On a hot, sunny February morning in Nairobi, close to 60 members of the [Ogiek](https://newint.org/features/2023/06/05/long-read-now-implementation-mau-forest-kenya-indigenous-decolonizehow) and Endorois Indigenous communities marched through the streets of the Kenyan capital chanting protest songs.

The group headed towards the Attorney General’s office to deliver a letter which challenged the government’s failure to implement court rulings that would compensate both communities and give them back their [stolen ancestral land](https://newint.org/issues/2023/02/08/take-back-land).

‘The document has been received, they have stamped our copy, which is evidence that we have presented our document today,’ explained head of the Endorois Community Welfare Council, Richard Kamworor.

![Image 1: Richard Kamworor](https://newint.org/sites/default/files/2024-02/ANT_1484.jpeg)

_Richard Kamworor, CEO of Endorois Welfare Council, marches with his community members during their land rights protest in Nairobi, Kenya on 6 February._

**A tale of two evictions**
---------------------------

The Kenyan government forcefully evicted the [Endorois](https://grist.org/global-indigenous-affairs-desk/indigenous-endorois-of-kenya-fight-for-their-land-and-rights-at-un/) people, a traditional pastoralist community, from their homes near the fertile lands of Lake Bogoria in central Kenya in the 1970s to make room for a game reserve and tourist facilities. Around 60,000 people were uprooted and forced to congregate on arid land, where many of their cattle died, devastating them economically, socially and culturally.

In 1986, the Endorois tried, unsuccessfully, to petition the Kenyan government to reverse its evictions policy. They were also denied any share in the revenue generated from tourism sector in the region.

Advert

[![Image 2: Newint - CHN Nov 25](https://static.ethicalshop.org/media/CandourFiles/CHN_reciprocal_SquareishNov25.jpg)](https://ead.newint.org/click.php?id=930)

When the Kenyan courts refused to address their case, the community went to the African Commission on Human and People’s Rights (ACHPR). In 2009 the court made a landmark ruling, considered a victory for [Indigenous peoples](https://newint.org/themes/indigenous-peoples#:~:text=Here%20you%20will%20find%20our,the%20destruction%20of%20their%20lands.) across Africa, ordering the Kenyan government to restore the Endorois to their historic land, compensate them from losses and to pay them profits from the Lake Bogoria game reserve.

But over a decade later, the Endorois are still waiting to return to their land.

THE IMPACTS OF Non-Implementation
---------------------------------

A 2022 [report](https://minorityrights.org/resources/implement-endorois-decision-276-03-report-on-the-impact-of-non-implementation-of-the-african-commissions-endorois-decision/) by Minority Rights Group found that the non-implementation of the Endorois decision has consigned many of its members to 'severe poverty, illiteracy, poor health and a life of destitution.'

The Endorois case was an important precursor to another landmark case at the ACHPR, this time brought by the Ogiek people who had experienced multiple evictions from their ancestral homes in the Mau Forest in south western Kenya. The Ogiek were first evicted by the British colonial government in 1920, with the latest evictions occurring at the hands of the Kenyan authorities last November [during the visit of Britain’s King Charles III](https://newint.org/features/2023/10/30/justice-king). Human rights lawyers say the government is also illegally evicting the Ogiek in order to [profit from carbon offsetting schemes](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-67352067). Seven-hundred households in Sasimwani in Narok County were targeted, including Judy Nagol’s.

‘I was evicted yet I was born in Sasimwani and even my grandparents were born there,’ she said. Nagol, who is disabled, now lives at a well-wisher's house in Olkirkirai, near the edge of the [forest](https://newint.org/themes/forests), with her three children.

![Image 3: Judy Nagol breaks down during the protest](https://newint.org/sites/default/files/2024-02/ANT_1403.jpeg)

_Judy Nagol, an Ogiek community member who was evicted from her home in November is overcome by emotion during the protests._

These latest evictions happened despite their success at the ACHPR. In 2017, the Court ordered the Kenyan government to restitute the Ogiek ancestral land and pay a compensation of 157,000 Kenyan shillings ($1,026) per person. But as in the case of the Endorois, the government has so far failed to implement the court’s orders, leaving many Ogiek unable to return to their rightful land.

'I am so sad to be here asking to be allowed to go back to my home.'

**‘We demand our land’**
------------------------

Fed up with the government’s inaction, the two communities came together in Nairobi on 6 February with the support of the International Network for Economic, Social and Cultural Rights to demand the government implement the rulings.

Nagol was among the protesters.

‘I am so sad to be here asking to be allowed to go back to my home,’ she said.

Speaking during the protest, Daniel Kobei, the Executive Director of the Ogiek People’s Development Programme said his community is angered by the continuous delays and that they have given the government three weeks to respond to their demands.

‘It is not to our liking to be in these streets in Nairobi,' he said. 'We could have been at home but because of this we have come to see the Attorney General for him to tell us why the implementation of the Endorois and Ogiek ruling has delayed. We demand our land, we demand for our rights.'

[Buffalo Human Rights Law Review](https://digitalcommons.law.buffalo.edu/bhrlr "Buffalo Human Rights Law Review")
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Rights
------

[![Image 1: In Copyright](https://rightsstatements.org/files/buttons/InC.dark-white-interior.png)](http://rightsstatements.org/vocab/InC/1.0/)

Abstract
--------

This article examines Communication 276/2003, Center for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group International on behalf of the Endorois Welfare Council v. Kenya, argued before the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. The Endorois Communication is one of the first indigenous rights claims to be examined by an international body after the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

This article begins by placing the Communication within the context of the international indigenous rights movement. The authors then explore the Commission's historical use of Articles 60 and 61 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. The authors contend that the Commission, while liberally deploying comparative jurisprudence from the European and Inter-American Human Rights systems, failed to articulate the bounds and import of Articles 60 and 61 of the African Charter. Finally, the authors propose that the Commission should have grafted the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into its understanding of long-standing African Charter rights through Articles 60 and 61. Despite the Commission's significant finding that Kenya violated the rights of the Endorois Community, the authors conclude that the Commission missed an opportunity to declare that the Charter's rights are only adequately applied to indigenous populations, through the framework of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Recommended Citation
--------------------

Korir S. Oei A. & Jared Shepherd, _In Land We Trust': The Endorois' Communication and the Quest for Indigenous Peoples' Rights in Africa_, 16 Buff. Hum. Rts. L. Rev. 57 (2010).  
Available at: https://digitalcommons.law.buffalo.edu/bhrlr/vol16/iss1/2

11.content:
**Image description: a legislative chamber hosting a summit of the African Union**

In June 2022, the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (“ACHPR”), [awarded](https://www.african-court.org/cpmt/storage/app/uploads/public/62b/aba/fd8/62babafd8d467689318212.pdf) USD 1.3 million to the Ogiek people of the Mau Forest. The amount must be paid by the Kenyan Government for breaching the rights of the Ogiek people by attempting to [evict](https://news.mongabay.com/2018/10/kenya-indigenous-ogiek-face-eviction-from-their-ancestral-forest-again/) them from their ancestral lands in the Mau Forest Complex. ACHPR also ruled that the Kenyan Government should recognize Ogiek as indigenous peoples (protected status), something which has been long resisted by the Government.

**History**

The Ogiek community are simple hunter-gatherers that have faced [evictions](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2016/aug/18/kenyas-ogiek-people-are-seeing-their-land-rights-brutalised) ever since the early 1930s to clear lands for British settlements. The community finally decided to [petition](https://minorityrights.org/2009/10/28/illegal-eviction-of-ogiek-indigenous-community-from-ancestral-home-in-mau-forest-kenya/) against a 30-day eviction notice that was served upon them in 2009. After 8 years of legal battle, the ACHPR finally [ruled](https://www.escr-net.org/sites/default/files/caselaw/ogiek_case_full_judgment.pdf) that the actions of the Kenyan government had violated the principles of non-discrimination (Article 2) and the right to religion (Article 8) and culture (Article 17) of the Ogiek people. However, the court did not rule on reparations, leaving the issue for a later decision.

**Indigenous Status**

The 2017 judgment recognized the indigenous status of the Ogiek people. The 2022 judgment affirmed this part of the judgment adding that the Kenyan Government must take sufficient measures to ensure the status of the Ogiek people. The judgment recognised the longstanding oppression and marginalisation of the Ogiek. This status is not a symbol of subordination, but it [recognizes](https://newleftreview.org/issues/ii3/articles/nancy-fraser-rethinking-recognition) that certain groups require institutional remedies for institutionalized harms. The Court stated that this recognition is not detached from the other claims of survival and livelihood but is intrinsically tied to it.

**Reparations**

The ACHPR awarded reparations to the Ogiek on two broad grounds. Firstly, for the material prejudice suffered by the Ogiek in the form of destruction of property and natural resources, KES 57,850,000 (USD 500,000) was awarded. Secondly, the Court recognized that there was moral prejudice to the Ogiek. The evictions were said to cause great distress to the families of Ogiek for which a compensation of KES 100,000,000 (USD 850,000) was awarded. On top of these compensations, non-monetary reparations were also awarded. Relying on the case of [_Centre for Minority Rights Development (Kenya) and Minority Rights Group (on behalf of the Endorois Welfare Council) v. Kenya_](https://www.achpr.org/sessions/descions?id=193), the Court said that under international law, mere access to land is not enough and there needs to be restitution of their ancestral lands.

**Consultations**

The judgment went further than merely adjudicating the issues that had already arisen. Citing the Inter-American Court of Human Rights _[Case of The Kichwa Indigenous People of Sarayaku v. Ecuador](https://corteidh.or.cr/docs/casos/articulos/seriec_245_ing.pdf)_, the Court said that there is an obligation to consult the Ogiek regarding all future developmental projects. This ruling sets an important precedent for other indigenous communities who are currently under threat of corporations and municipal bodies dictating the future of their land. If the Ogiek and the third party are unable to reach an agreement on the future of the land, then according to the judgment, the land would have to be returned to the Ogiek.

**Impact**

It is a general trend of governments around the world to marginalise the indigenous communities, forcing them to fight for their rights in courts. There will always be a mismatch of resources between the communities and the state which would further aggravate their struggles. The [Ogiek Peoples’ Development Program](https://www.forestpeoples.org/en/press-release/06-2022/ogiek-kenya-celebrate-reparations-judgement) remarked that the long court battles negatively impact the community’s capacity to focus on their own social and economical development. This judgment is monumental not only for Ogiek but for indigenous communities across Africa. By relying on the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People, the Court concretized the rights of vulnerable groups that require special protection. Lastly, by recognizing that the indigenous groups cannot be held responsible for the depletion of forest resources, the Court eliminated any grounds that justified the eviction of the Ogiek people.

Want to learn more?

*   Listen: [A Historic Moment: The Drafting of the New Chilean Constitution](https://ohrh.law.ox.ac.uk/a-historic-moment-the-drafting-of-the-new-chilean-constitution/)
*   Read: [Climate Change and the Torres Strait Islands: Australia in the International Spotlight](https://ohrh.law.ox.ac.uk/climate-change-and-the-torres-strait-islands-australia-in-the-international-spotlight/)

![Image 1: Endorois Indigenous Women Empowerment Network – EIWEN](blob:https://www.escr-net.org/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)

Endorois Indigenous Women Empowerment Network - EIWEN

**What is this case about?**
----------------------------

In the 1970s, the Kenyan government evicted hundreds of Endorois families from their traditional lands around the Lake Bogoria area in the Rift Valley, to create a game reserve for tourism. In response, and after pursuing legal options at the national level, the **Endorois Welfare Council**, assisted by fellow ESCR-Net members, **Minority Rights Group International** and the **Center for Minority Rights Development**, took the case to the African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights (ACHPR). In 2010, the ACHPR issued a judgment stating that the Kenyan government had violated the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, specifically the rights to religious practice, to property, to culture, to the free disposition of natural resources, and to development. While certain aspects of the Commission decision have been realized, the Kenyan government has mostly not complied with the recommendations yet. The case represents the first legal recognition of an African indigenous peoples’ rights over traditionally owned land and is also the first case globally which found a violation of the right to development. For a full case summary, please click [**here**](https://www.escr-net.org/caselaw/2010/centre-minority-rights-development-kenya-and-minority-rights-group-international-behalf/?_rt=M3wxfGVuZG9yb2lzfDE3MTg5OTcwNjQ&_rt_nonce=49be2dbedb).

**What collective implementation activity took place?**
-------------------------------------------------------

ESCR-Net members worked in close partnership and solidarity with members and allies based both in Kenya and beyond, to advance implementation of the specific decision and land-related rights generally. Throughout the implementation efforts, particular emphasis has been placed on the role of women in progressing implementation and in engaging and taking leadership roles in land rights more broadly. Collective efforts include:

*   Community workshops conducted in 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2018 with Strategic Litigation Working Group (SLWG) members, **Minority Rights Group International**, **Dejusticia** (Colombia), **Hakijamii** (Kenya), **Kenya Human Rights Commission** (Kenya), **Kenya Land Alliance** (Kenya), **Ogiek Peoples’ Development Program** (Kenya) and **Center for Minority Rights Development** (CEMIRIDE), among others, regarding issues of compensation, restitution, registration, community bylaws, and women’s leadership
*   Various strategic exchanges with community members and allies, and [**engagement with the ACHPR**](https://www.escr-net.org/news/2017/escr-net-sends-letter-to-the-achpr-regarding-land-restitution-for-the-endorois/), the [**government task force**](https://www.escr-net.org/news/2014/first-meeting-of-the-kenyan-task-force-for-the-implementation-of-the-endorois-decision/) (created in 2014 with a one-year mandate to study the implementation of the Endorois decision) as well as various government agencies
*   A survey on immaterial losses connected with the eviction, to support negotiations with the government regarding a monetary amount to compensate the community for such losses
*   The formulation of a draft Endorois community membership code (to provide criteria for identifying who may be recognised as a member of the Endorois community).

**Key documents:**
------------------

*   Claimants’ **[admissibility submission on the admissibility of the case](http://minorityrights.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Final-admissibility-pleading.pdf)** (English only)
*   Claimants’ **[submission on the merits of the case](http://minorityrights.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/CEMIRIDE-on-behalf-of-the-Endorois-Community-Communication-276.pdf)** (English only)
*   The ACHPR’s **[decision on the case](http://www.achpr.org/communications/decision/276.03/)** (English only)
*   The ACHPR **[Resolution](http://www.achpr.org/sessions/54th/resolutions/257/)** calling on the Republic of Kenya to implement the Endorois decision (2O13) (English, French, Arabic and Portuguese)
*   CESCR’s **[Concluding Observations](http://tbinternet.ohchr.org/_layouts/treatybodyexternal/Download.aspx?symbolno=E%2fC.12%2fKEN%2fCO%2f2-5&Lang=en)** on the combined second to fifth periodic reports of Kenya (2016), paras. 15-16 (English, French, Spanish and Arabic)
*   Open Society Justice Initiative, **[Strategic Litigation Impacts: Indigenous Peoples’ Land Rights](https://www.opensocietyfoundations.org/reports/strategic-litigation-impacts-indigenous-peoples-land-rights)** (2017) – for a summary of the case and commentary on its specific and wider impacts
*   ESCR-Net, **[The Emerging Leadership of Endorois Women: An Indirect Impact of the Endorois Case](https://www.escr-net.org/resources/the-emerging-leadership-of-endorois-women-an-indirect-impact-of-the-endorois-case/)** (2019)
